Wingspan Bird Tier List

Wingspan Bird Tier List

This is a tier list of every bird in Wingspan's digital edition, including all the expansions and promo packs, ranked by a computer player. We built a computer player for Wingspan and had it play 470,000 three-player games against copies of itself. Then we looked at every bird a player drew blind off the deck and asked one question: did the players who got that bird end up further ahead than the players who got some other bird? The answer, in points, is the number under each card. Each tab is a separate list. Pick one, then tap a card for details.

The number is the bird's effect on your final margin (your score minus your best opponent's), compared with an average bird in its place. Nobody chooses the top card of the deck, so across thousands of games everything else washes out and the difference belongs to the bird.

Values by stage. Each bird has five values: one for the starting hand (kept on a coin flip here, so luck again) and one per round. White Stork is +7.7 in the starting hand, +3.6 in round 2 and +1.2 in round 4. The card's number blends the five, leaning on the early rounds because more birds are gained then. Tap a card for all five.

Based on 470,000 games, all played by the computer against copies of itself.

Surprises

  • The base game's famous "Power 4", Common Raven, Chihuahuan Raven, Franklin's Gull and Killdeer, all come out below average on the Oceania mats.
  • Point bombs rule. Every bird worth 8 or 9 points is above average, and they stay strong right through round 4.
  • Bonus-card birds are the big winners. Six of the ten best birds in the game draw bonus cards.
  • Wood Duck and Spangled Drongo are the best birds in the game to find in a starting hand, and nearly worthless by round 2.
  • An extra turn is worth about 4 points, and every extra bird kept in the opening hand is worth about a point.

All birds: Birds

Click a column heading to sort by it. A bird's true value very likely lies within the margin of error on either side of the number shown.

Value
the bird's effect on your final margin, in points, against an average bird drawn in its place
Margin of error
the true value very likely lies this far either side of the number
Plays per 100 games
how often the computer played it, counting all three players
Forced play
now and then the computer was made to play a bird at random instead of the one it wanted. This is the average change in its final margin when the random pick was this bird. Near zero means it was about as good as the computer's choice, and a large negative number means the computer was right to pass it over
Usual round
the average round in which the computer played it
Points it scores when played
printed points plus the eggs, cached food and tucked cards on it at game end

The number is the bonus card's effect on your final margin, compared with an average bonus card, measured in the same games and the same way as the birds. Bonus cards arrive blind too, dealt at the start or drawn by a bird's power, so the players who got a given card can be fairly compared with the players who got another. It counts the chance to keep the card, so a card the computer usually discards scores near zero at best.

Fine print

  • Small differences don't mean much. Each value is good to about ±0.05 points, so cards a tenth of a point apart are effectively tied.
  • Kept when dealt is the share of the times the card was offered and the computer chose to keep it. Points when kept is the card's average score at game end.
  • A strong computer player's values. These come from the same 470,000 three-player games as the bird list, played by the newest version of the computer player on the Oceania mats with nectar. Nobody can promise the computer plays perfectly, but it plays well.

The computer player and the community tier lists

  • Wood Duck is as good as people say. Wingsplain's tier list puts Wood Duck in its top "God Tier", and Board Game Arena forum posters call it the strongest card outside the banned list and dead weight if drawn late. The computer agrees on all of it. Wood Duck is the third-best base-game bird and the best bird in the game to find in a starting hand (+9.5), and it is worth nothing in round 4. The computer also agrees with Wingsplain that Galah, Grey Butcherbird and Sacred Kingfisher are good Oceania birds, and that New Holland Honeyeater belongs near the bottom.
  • The "Power 4" are overrated. Common Raven, Chihuahuan Raven, Franklin's Gull and Killdeer top the King Panda Games base-game list and an R-bloggers card analysis, and Steam forum players call the Raven overpowered. On the Oceania mats, the computer rates all four below average, from −0.5 for Franklin's Gull to −1.0 for Killdeer. It still plays Common Raven about as often as an average bird, yet once its printed points are set aside, the Raven's power rates third-worst in the game. Nobody can promise the computer plays perfectly, and it learned only from games against copies of itself. But it is a strong player, and here the human consensus looks wrong for the Oceania game. All four turn your own eggs into food or cards, and that trade seems to have lost its value. Wingsplain's own notes call the Oceania game "egg-starved", and eggs make up only a ninth of the computer's score.
  • Many fan favorites are overrated. Maned Duck, Noisy Miner, Common Chiffchaff and Rainbow Lorikeet sit high on Wingsplain's list and near the bottom of this one, and the computer almost never plays them. Base-game favorites from forum threads and top-10 articles, such as Spotted Towhee, Gray Catbird, Anna's Hummingbird and Green Heron, also land below average. These reputations come from the base game, and on the Oceania mats the birds look weaker than their fame.

Patterns across the whole deck

  • Point bombs are great. Every one of the 28 birds worth 8 or 9 points is above average, and they stay strong right through round 4. Of everything on the card apart from the power, printed points matter most.
  • The power matters more than the body. Points, egg limit, habitats, nest, wingspan and food cost together explain only about a quarter of the differences between birds. The power explains the rest. With the rest of the card held equal, each printed point adds about 0.16, and each nectar in the cost takes away almost half a point. Food cost is no drawback: an extra food in the cost goes with slightly more value, about a tenth of a point.
  • Small egg limits are better. Birds with an egg limit of 0 or 1 average +0.7, and birds with a limit of 4 or more average −0.3. The gap holds at the same point value. The bonus cards for big egg piles, Oologist and Breeding Manager, are weak too.
  • Bonus-card birds are the big winners. Six of the ten best birds in the game draw bonus cards, five in six birds with a bonus-card power are above average, and they grow stronger as the game goes on. Fittingly, Endangered Species Protector, the bonus card for exactly these birds, is the best bonus card by a wide margin.
  • Nectar birds are weak. Nearly every bird with nectar in its cost is below average, and the computer almost never plays them. Spangled Drongo is the exception: it is the second-best card to find in a starting hand.
  • Promo birds are the strongest. The promo packs beat the base game and every expansion, even at the same point value. The base game and the three expansions are about equal to one another. The New Zealand and Asia packs are the best, and the UK pack is the only weak one.
  • Card-flipping predators are strong. Predators that flip a card from the deck are above average on the whole, and predators that roll dice are merely average. Every eagle in the game is above average.

Near-twin cards

  • Extra habitats add value. On birds with the same power, each extra habitat is worth about a quarter of a point, and some cases are far bigger. Chipping Sparrow (forest or grassland) beats Grasshopper, Baird's and Cassin's Sparrows (grassland only) by nearly 2 points with identical cost and power. Three-habitat House Finch likewise beats wetland-only Tree Swallow.
  • On the same power, more printed points help. Many base-game birds share "draw 2 new bonus cards and keep 1". All of them are above average, and the more points printed on the card, the better the bird, from King Rail near zero up to 8-point Atlantic Puffin at +3.2. Each extra printed point adds about a third of a point of value, and 4-point Bell's Vireo (+2.3) is the odd one out. White Stork, the best bird in the game, shares its tray-refresh power with two weaker birds, and its 8 points make the difference.
  • Tuckers need a draw. Brown birds that tuck a card from your hand and draw a replacement are mostly above average. The ones with no draw are mostly below average, and two of them, Eurasian Coot and Maned Duck, are among the weakest cards in the game. Ruff, which draws a card for every card it tucks, is excellent.

Peak rounds

  • Pink birds peak in the starting hand. Pink birds are the strongest color at three players, but their value comes early. They are superb starting-hand cards and slightly below average by round 4. White birds climb from below average in the starting hand to solidly positive later. Yellow birds are the worst color to open with.
  • Some birds are only good early. Wood Duck, Spangled Drongo, Laughing Gull and California Scrub-Jay are among the best starting-hand cards in the game and worth nothing in round 4. The late bloomers are big when-played birds. Giant Fish Owl, Steppe Eagle and Sulu Hornbill are the three best birds to draw in round 4.

Power families

  • "Play an additional bird" powers are weak. Not one bird whose power lets you play an additional bird at its normal cost is above average. Players prize the saved action, and the computer may underrate it, but at three players it rarely finds these birds worth playing. Yellow-Eyed Penguin is the lone exception at +2.0, and the difference is the word "free".
  • "All players" powers hurt. Brown birds worth 6 points or more with a power that gives every player the same thing average about half a point less than other brown birds of their size, and the gift is the main reason some 7-point birds are bad. Giving to one chosen opponent hurts less than giving to everyone. At two players the cost should shrink.
  • Free dice are gold. Pink birds that take a die from the birdfeeder on other players' turns are above average, Eurasian Wren (+2.8) and Laughing Gull especially. The one exception is Boat-Tailed Grackle, which must first cache a food from your supply. Powers that give one named food are below average, and none of the base-game jays and woodpeckers that take "1 seed from the birdfeeder, if available" is above average.
  • Spending food for points loses. Brown powers that spend food to tuck cards, lay eggs or draw cards are a losing trade, and nearly all of them sit below average. Free caching works: every base-game chickadee and nuthatch that caches a seed from the supply is above average despite its small points.
  • Card draws pay early. Powers that draw several cards and let you keep one are excellent in the starting hand and below average from round 2 on. Mandarin Duck and Australian Ibis are the best of them. Powers that simply draw a card into your hand are all below average.
  • Round-end and game-end egg powers are weak. Teal and yellow birds that lay eggs are the weakest birds of their colors, and not one yellow egg-layer is above average. The "lay 1 egg on each of your birds" family is weak at every color, with Say's Phoebe (+0.9) the clear best of them.
  • Some powers go unplayed. Several whole families sit near the bottom because the computer almost never plays them: birds that move themselves to another habitat, birds that copy another bird's power, and the teal birds that count double toward the end-of-round goal. These values mostly reflect the computer's refusal, and a player with a good copy target in view may do better with them. Birds played less than once per 100 games carry a grey "rarely played" flag in the list, and their order among themselves means little.
  • The raptors played on top are a special case. Red Kite, Eurasian Hobby, Montagu's Harrier and Common Buzzard, the European birds played on top of another bird, are now four of the six lowest birds in the game. The computer does play them, about three times per 100 games, and its own estimate of its position drops about 2 points right after it does. It seems to play them badly, so a player who picks the right bird to cover may get more from them.

Bird families

  • Cuckoos are excellent. The cuckoos and cowbirds that lay on another bird when a rival takes the lay-eggs action are nearly all above average, led by Asian Koel, Violet Cuckoo and Common Cuckoo. The computer plays them about twice as often as an average bird, and they are best drawn in rounds 1 and 2.
  • Flightless birds are excellent. The kiwis and penguins are among the best cards in the game, and Takahē and Weka are well above average too. Kākāpō comes out average (but see the random plays below), and Emu and Southern Cassowary fall short.
  • Geese, herons and starlings disappoint. Geese and swans carry plenty of printed points and still mostly come out below average, with Greater Snow Goose the best of them. Herons and egrets are weak too, apart from Black-crowned Night-Heron. Starlings and mynas are below average except Bali Starling, a bonus-card bird. Ducks are all over the place, from Wood Duck and Mandarin Duck near the top to Maned Duck and Common Teal near the bottom.

Nests, wingspans and food costs

  • Star nests are best. Birds whose nest counts as any type do clearly better than birds with a fixed nest, by about 0.4 points at the same points and egg limit. End-of-round goals and bonus cards keyed to nest types reward a nest that counts as all of them, though these birds may also simply have better powers.
  • Wingspan doesn't matter. At the same point value, big and small birds come out the same, and the bonus cards keyed to wingspan are poor. Big wingspans simply come with big points.
  • Food type barely matters. Birds paid in rodents or fish do a little better than birds paid in invertebrates, and birds paid entirely in seed do a little worse, mostly because the computer rarely plays them. Wild food in the cost makes no difference, and the flexible "or" cost is no bargain.

Expansions, colors and habitats

  • A printed point is worth more in the expansions. Each extra printed point on a bird adds the least value in the base game and the most in the European expansion, more than twice as much. The base game's big birds suffer most, for two reasons. Its birds with no power at all, such as Wild Turkey and Trumpeter Swan, trail powered birds of the same points by nearly a point, and its many brown "all players" birds are weak at every point value.
  • European round-end birds are weak. The European expansion introduced the teal round-end power, and its own teal birds are the weakest version of it. Ruff is the big exception. The Asian and promo teal birds do much better, led by Sri Lanka Blue-Magpie, Tufted Puffin and Great Spotted Kiwi.
  • Brown grassland birds are the weakest. Brown birds that live only in grassland are the weakest habitat-and-color group in the game, and a third of them are rarely played. Brown forest and wetland birds do better, and white grassland birds are fine. Nearly the only brown grassland birds that pay are predators such as Greater Roadrunner. The rest mostly lay or trade eggs, and egg powers lose value on the Oceania mats.

Timing and the tray

  • The starting hand matters most. Birds differ almost four times as much in value in the starting hand as in round 4. Keeping a dealt Wood Duck instead of discarding it is worth 10 points, and keeping Brahminy Starling, the worst opener, costs about 2.5. No bird drawn in round 4 costs even 1. So the opening keep is the decision to sweat over.
  • Printed points barely matter in the starting hand. Big and small birds are nearly even as starting-hand cards, and from round 2 on the number in the corner becomes the best single guide to a bird's value. Early, the power decides: pink birds and brown card-drawers make the best opening keeps.
  • Brown card-drawers fade. Brown birds that draw cards are excellent in the starting hand and slightly below average by round 4. Birds with "all players" powers are a real liability in the starting hand, since the gift to opponents adds up over a whole game, and harmless by round 4.
  • Round-1 filler is weak. The computer plays nearly 30% of its birds in round 1, and the cheap brown birds it plays almost only then are mostly below average. Human players prize a cheap round-1 engine, and some of these cards may do more in human hands, but here they look like plays made for lack of anything better.
  • The tray is a bargain bin. Birds nobody wants sit face up until someone takes them, so nearly two-thirds of the birds on offer in the tray come from the bottom half of this list. The computer picks accordingly. It takes an S-tier bird 84% of the time one is on offer and an F-tier bird about 1% of the time, and when it was forced to take a bottom-tier bird, it lost nearly a point against its own pick.
  • A strong bird in a rival's hand costs you half its value. When an opponent draws a bird, your final margin moves by about half the bird's value in the other direction. A rival's White Stork costs you 2.2 points. So a great bird taken from the tray also keeps it from the next player.

Turns, actions and the opening

  • Keep birds over food. In these games the starting birds were kept on a coin flip, so the value of each kept bird shows directly. Every extra bird kept, with one less food, is worth about a point of final margin. Players who kept all five birds finished about 5 points better off than players who kept none. The first kept bird adds 1.7 points and the fifth only 0.4.
  • Keep invertebrates and seed. Against the average starting food, a kept invertebrate is worth +0.3 and a seed +0.2. Fruit is average, and fish (−0.2) and rodent (−0.3) are the worst foods to keep.
  • A turn is worth about 4 points. The Oceania "no goal" tile lets everyone keep that round's goal cube, so every later round has one more turn. With no goal in round 1, players scored 10.7 points more than average, from three extra turns and despite the missing goal. With no goal in round 4 there is no extra turn, and players scored 4.6 points less. Counting the goal points given up, each extra turn is worth about 4 points.
  • Playing a bird is the best action in every round. Now and then the computer had to take a random action. Against an average random action, playing a bird gained 0.7 to 1.2 points in every round. Drawing cards is good in round 1 (+0.4) and the worst action in round 4 (−1.2). Laying eggs runs the other way: the worst action in round 1 (−0.8) and the second best in round 4 (+0.5). The computer's own choice beat every one of these fixed actions, and a random action other than the one it wanted cost it 1.2 to 2.1 points.
  • Bird cards carry the score. The computer averages 95 points a game, and 44 of them come from the birds' printed points. Bonus cards, end-of-round goals and eggs bring about 11 points each, and nectar, tucked cards and cached food bring the rest.
  • The first player's edge is small. The first seat wins 34.4% of three-player games and the third seat 31.7%, a gap of about a point of final margin.

Random bird plays

  • The computer's picks are worth about a point and a half. One time in fifty, the computer had to play a random bird from the ones it could afford. Against its own choice from the same kind of hand, a random play cost it about 1.4 points on a typical bird, and for most birds the random play did clearly worse.
  • Three blind spots. For Kākāpō, Laughing Gull and Yellow-Eyed Penguin, a random play of the bird did better than the computer's own choice, by 1.3 to 1.9 points. They are the only birds with a gap larger than its margin of error. Kākāpō's average value mostly reflects the computer's reluctance to play it, less than twice per 100 games. A forced Kākāpō beat a random playable bird by over 4 points, so it may well be better than its tier when you can afford it.
  • Some birds are traps. A forced play of European Serin, Common Moorhen, Short-Toed Treecreeper or Killdeer did 4 to 6 points worse than a random playable bird. The computer is right to pass them over.

Bonus cards

  • A bonus card is only as good as its birds. Bonus cards for strong groups of birds are strong, as with Diet Specialist (three-food birds), Rodentologist and Falconer. Bonus cards for weak groups are weak, as with Backyard Birder (low-point birds) and Bird Feeder (seed-eaters). Cartographer is the exception: its birds are ordinary, but a few birds with geography terms in their names already pay off.
  • Player-mat bonus cards hold up late. Bonus cards for a kind of bird lose value as the game goes on, since there is less time left to collect. Falconer falls from +1.0 in the starting hand to +0.2 in round 4. Cards that score the shape of your player mat hold their value or gain, since they pay for a mat you already have. Mechanical Engineer and Ethologist are strong at every stage.
  • Bonus cards need 3 points. A bonus card that won't reach about 3 points is a net loss. The worst ones pay for leftovers or for runs: Visionary Leader (bird cards left in hand) is the worst in the box, with Winter Feeder and the Ranger and Data Analyst cards close behind. Endangered Species Protector, Ethologist, Mechanical Engineer and Ecologist are the best.

Changes from the first version

  • Bonus-card birds rose. The first version of this list came from 150,000 games of an older computer player on an earlier version of the game engine. The two lists rank birds much the same way, with some notable moves. Abbott's Booby rose from +0.7 to +2.1, and New Zealand Rock Wren, Giant Fish Owl, Steppe Eagle and Sulu Hornbill each rose by about a point. Galah fell from +2.2 to +0.8, Yellow-Eyed Penguin from +3.1 to +2.0, and Willow Warbler from +1.0 to about zero.
  • No single cause. The computer player, the engine fixes and the random exploration all changed between the two versions, so no single change can be credited with any bird's move.

Fine print

  • Small differences don't mean much. Each value is good to about ±0.14 points, so birds a few tenths apart are effectively tied. Ranking each half of the games separately gives nearly the same list (the two halves correlate at 0.99).
  • Tray picks are left out. The numbers come only from birds that arrive face down: drawn from the deck, by the draw-cards action or by a bird's power, or dealt into the starting hand. A bird taken from the tray is a choice, so the players who take it aren't a fair comparison. The same goes for a card picked from several drawn by a power. Most cards arrive blind anyway: 93% of the bird cards that reached a hand came straight off the deck.
  • A sharper reading. Each finish is measured against the computer's own guess of it, made just before the card came off the deck. The guess comes before the card, so it can't favor any bird, and it stops a runaway leader from flattering the card they happened to draw.
  • A strong computer player's values. These come from 470,000 three-player games of the newest version of the computer player against copies of itself. It learned the game on its own, with no strategy advice from people. Nobody can promise it plays perfectly, but it plays well, and its disagreements with popular opinion (more on those above) deserve a hearing. In these games it also kept its starting birds on a coin flip, made one tray pick in five at random, and one time in fifty took a random action or played a random bird, so it played a little below its usual level. Those random moves are the source of several findings above.
  • Three-player games on the Oceania mats with nectar. Birds whose worth depends on the number of opponents, pink powers for example, could rank differently at two or four players.
  • Every bird is here. All 586 birds of the digital edition are in the list, including the four birds played sideways, Rock Ptarmigan, Ivory Gull and Black-and-White Warbler, which the first version lacked.
  • Tap any card for a larger view, its value and margin of error, its value at each stage, and the rounds the computer tends to play it in.
